'''William Ernest Johnson''' (23 June 1858 – 14 January 1931), usually cited as '''W. E. Johnson''', was a British [[philosopher]], [[logician]] and [[economic theorist]].<ref name=":4">Zabell, S.L. (2008) [https://books.google.com/books?id=EO40DAAAQBAJ&pg=RA3-PA640 "Johnson, William Ernest (1858–1931)"] In: Durlauf S.N., Blume L.E. (eds) ''[[The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics]].''(2nd ed, 2008.) Palgrave Macmillan, London {{Doi|10.1007/978-1-349-58802-2_868}}</ref> He is mainly remembered for his 3 volume ''Logic'' which introduced the concept of [[Exchangeable random variables|exchangeability]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zabell |first=S. L. |date=1992 |title=Predicting the Unpredictable |url=https://www.ece.uvic.ca/~bctill/papers/mocap/Zabell_1991.pdf |journal=Synthese |language=en |volume=90 |issue=2 [pp. 205–232] |pages=229 |doi=10.1007/BF00485351 |issn=0039-7857 |s2cid=9416747}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Zabell|first=Sandy L.|date=1982|title=W. E. Johnson's "Sufficientness" Postulate|journal=The Annals of Statistics|language=en|volume=10|issue=4 [pp.1090–1099]|pages=1097, 1099|doi=10.1214/aos/1176345975|issn=0090-5364|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Johnson was born in Cambridge on 23 June 1858 to William Henry Farthing Johnson and his wife, Harriet (''née'' Brimley), half-sister of the essayist [[George Brimley]].<ref name=":0" /> He was their fifth child.<ref name=":0" /> The family were Baptists and political liberals.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Broad |first=C. D. |date=1931 |title=William Ernest Johnson |url=https://www.thebritishacademy.ac.uk/documents/5229/17p491.pdf |journal=[[Proceedings of the British Academy]] |volume=17 |pages=94–114}}</ref>

He attended the Llandaff House School, Cambridge where his father was the proprietor and headteacher, then the [[The Perse School|Perse School]], Cambridge, and the Liverpool Royal Institution School.<ref name=":0">{{cite ODNB |url=http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/DNB/Johnson.html |title=Johnson, William Ernest (1858–1931) |last1=Braithwaite |first1=R. B. |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/34206 |year=2004 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190609124743/http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/DNB/Johnson.html |archive-date=9 June 2019 |url-status=dead}}</ref> At the age of around eight he became seriously ill and developed severe asthma and lifelong ill health. Due to this his education was frequently disrupted.<ref name=":1" />

In 1879 he entered [[King's College, Cambridge]] to read mathematics having won a scholarship and was placed 11th [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Wrangler]] in 1882.<ref name=":2" /> He stayed on to study for the Moral Sciences Tripos from which he graduated in 1883 with a First Class degree.<ref name=":2">{{acad|id=JHN878WE|name=Johnson, William Ernest}}</ref> He was also a [[Cambridge Apostle]].<ref>First semester. (2017). In P. Bogaard & J. Bell (Eds.), ''The Harvard Lectures of Alfred North Whitehead, 1924–1925: Philosophical Presuppositions of Science'' (fn. 5. [https://books.google.com/books?id=dDVYDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA493 p. 493]). Edinburgh University Press.</ref>

In 1895 he married Barbara Keymer. After her sudden death in 1904 his sister Fanny moved in with him to care for his two sons.<ref name=":0" />

Having failed to win a prize fellowship, he taught mathematics. His first teaching post was as a lecturer in Psychology and Education at the [[Hughes Hall, Cambridge#History|Cambridge Women's Training College]], which he held for several years.<ref name=":1" /> He was a University Teacher of Theory of Education 1893–1898 and, from 1896 until 1901, University Lecturer in Moral Sciences at the [[University of Cambridge]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> In 1902 he was elected a [[Fellow]] of [[King's College, Cambridge|King's College]], and appointed to the newly created [[Henry Sidgwick|Sidgwick]] Lectureship, positions he held until his death.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" /> In 1923 he was elected a Fellow of the [[British Academy]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" />

Johnson's students included [[I. A. Richards]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Russo |first=John Paul |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h3PbCQAAQBAJ&q=johnson |title=I. A. Richards: His Life and Work |publisher=Routledge |year=2015 |isbn=9781138842717 |location=London |pages=46 |oclc=898154256 |quote=Richards' supervisor in moral science for his "last two years, nearly" ... W. E. Johnson ... was important "not so much for any one thing, but in the general intellectual rigor and imagination brought to bear upon issues." He was a "quiet, gentle man" who suffered badly from asthma. When Richards went to King's for supervision he would often find him lying in bed and would take notes from a man "quietly delivering monologues." Compared with McTaggart ... Johnson was "more judicious, more balanced, more interested in trying to say and restate what others thought. McTaggart was ... always trying to push his theories..."  ... Johnson's were "lessons in intellectual integrity.}}</ref> [[Dorothy Maud Wrinch|Dorothy Wrinch]],<ref name=":3" /> [[C. D. Broad]],<ref name=":4" /> [[R. B. Braithwaite]]<ref name=":1" /> and [[Susan Stebbing]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wisdom |first=John |date=1944 |title=L. Susan Stebbing, 1885–1943 |journal=Mind |volume=53 |issue=211 |pages=283–285 |doi=10.1093/mind/LIII.211.283 |issn=0026-4423 |jstor=2250468}}</ref> [[Frank P. Ramsey|Frank Ramsey]] is sometimes described as one of his students. However, as John Aldrich notes, Johnson lectured to, and supervised, moral science students and had no official duties toward students of mathematics and there is no evidence Ramsey attended his lectures.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Aldrich |first=John |date=February 2022 |title=W.E. Johnson and Cambridge thought on probability |url=https://pdf.sciencedirectassets.com/271876/1-s2.0-S0888613X21X00126/1-s2.0-S0888613X21001754/main.pdf?X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjELz%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2FwEaCXVzLWVhc3QtMSJGMEQCIF8zfBSeTo2W1yM1zKKeHQBSluat1TZcatz48IeRDlzTAiBd3D1PL%2BvehA0BH%2FXSROhpo0hdv%2BJxMIbBPKHYeNXJhSq7BQiE%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F8BEAUaDDA1OTAwMzU0Njg2NSIMiiCGWZVbLNAwwRiMKo8FDKzCAX80Nre4qo2ehhsRrYPWe6wupbXb4GuLh5apyYsa%2FF7hZA7CKbeHh70uhtVqY8Ik60BG3w9R4MfhEYRsagvGu42TYY4gI5s2jazo48DqgSOuWhMII32K77Q%2Bfa%2Fcr2zcfnKf0LyHF7lYvUKnQcPgy5q5Ymjr5lZLcWLknThH5ALJiS20%2B%2FYXNuUqUXJ2hCeJCPZUCkUagTbFDUIr9Y6RrmOpfuJxGN8ETTab9lUNBtcaewpWFNsnTB3sK4byS1Kd2dUhklzyubn5dGjj0O00aSN%2FZG9KQC3Q5hrswQwkJE2YyfgTfEbGMTSYSDTNH7jKohV20y60Q0aOGczpICoEzYvcWY1zi%2By23P%2BSZhd6GUv4Wm6YpH7W%2FrHosr%2FpGfFlkuxeWmZIKNeYrM2QBARQikkZKxQ4b%2B323xSORM3DG6Wb7HldOQYuHvBc8PGd5entaivIDOUtnPTRmPFydo9sI18yDKFnwLWKFt6TmgKj4fRAcVg0jfcBNLev6AfmqvWhWRRclM1i63cEAYY8DZJ1u5oeJ%2F4vYnwqsiYFk0yMEuxKpzg3MgfgPcZ%2Blyw1q9LxVekqH8PbtJ3SVoOz%2BxZxQFGN8dqg0bMcm0h7t0ydajHzFMpOqkuUM89WogEUU4jTwN0sUPQ4eg1yRh5SeJbZOdtIVBdG4qmJMXInyDvcstkNr%2B4%2Fv7wfvV3yOq2ZLD%2B5ww9H4WF2CVsEgUdd%2B0lJto58ZGFQBpOVwswqgqe7SGZ8yWKCnRL4M%2BezwjtrsSoLuy93Lh5PgHQ15CuPTkS5zbolT0UEUOEWqn%2Fj1DY5KlDlwvNO2P0dY0jPp%2BAx7TeFoJ6V1j5ONir%2FRaXT3o7vmnHChj8Hssh9hKDpAjCGxb7OBjqyAbGlh5ZCU49psG0o03BuGu9FD5ytqEyRfF2kb7DY%2FA3dpYb4kYYmkVC%2BkMuIaIdj5sT9qWvhoTpsowCEE18GGLtzQX1tGszl1EqJZswivPHqFF2KM2sorQRJBWbudKarQA60lFprJKZ4BYtU2qD3htHPIbwLFxefVPu3f8EL%2FegOnz%2BLLS6gN2AhLzP5p3xdbHhmGyhuZvnzSjNETN%2BuKB67vm1qf95utxNqIgClwXCDmLs%3D&X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Date=20260403T124232Z&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&X-Amz-Expires=300&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAQ3PHCVTYZMJTB4TK%2F20260403%2Fus-east-1%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Signature=f2351a11b7f2fd79145ffa763428d9025860a080aae392106976de65cec8c7f0&hash=365ac92432e2f70cb463fd4d129dba717d9ed422109f5413de40bc639ca361b8&host=68042c943591013ac2b2430a89b270f6af2c76d8dfd086a07176afe7c76c2c61&pii=S0888613X21001754&tid=spdf-84190086-aa24-4a0d-8397-cd100887bb3a&sid=666a3ace5b76e348ba99dfd51d66fdc878c0gxrqb&type=client&tsoh=d3d3LnNjaWVuY2VkaXJlY3QuY29t&rh=d3d3LnNjaWVuY2VkaXJlY3QuY29t&ua=07065f0a5459505252&rr=9e68275d48ca6349&cc=gb |journal=[[International Journal of Approximate Reasoning]] |language=en |volume=141 |pages=155 |doi=10.1016/j.ijar.2021.10.010|doi-access=free}}</ref> Ramsey though, as Sahlin notes, "knew the work of Johnson extremely well".<ref name=":9">{{Cite book |last=Sahlin |first=Nils-Eric |url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/The_Philosophy_of_F_P_Ramsey/_QwGuE2UD9IC?hl=en&gbpv=1&&pg=PA56 |title=The Philosophy of F. P. Ramsey |date=1990-08-31 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-38543-5 |pages=56-57 |language=en |quote=}}</ref> He would review the second part of Johnson's ''Logic'' in 1922 and referred to Johnson multiple times in his 1925 paper on 'Universals'.<ref>[[Frank Ramsey (mathematician)|F. P. Ramsey]], [[iarchive:sim_new-statesman_1922-07-29_19_485/page/469/mode/1up|"Review of W. E. Johnson's Logic Part II"]] ''[[New Statesman|The New Statesman]]'', 19 (July 1922), pp. 469–470.</ref>

In 1912 (at [[Bertrand Russell]]'s request) Johnson attempted to 'coach' [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]] in logic but this was an arrangement that was both brief and unsuccessful.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Monk, Ray. |url=https://archive.org/details/ludwigwittgenste0000monk_p1p1/page/42/mode/1up |title=Ludwig Wittgenstein: The Duty of Genius |date=1991 |publisher=Vintage |isbn=0099883708 |location=London |pages=42 |oclc=877368486 |quote=On 1 February 1912 Wittgenstein was admitted as a member of Trinity College, with Russell as his supervisor. Knowing that he had never received any formal tuition in logic, and feeling that he might benefit from it, Russell arranged for him to be ‘coached’ by the eminent logician and Fellow of King’s College, W. E. Johnson. The arrangement lasted only a few weeks. Wittgenstein later told F. R. Leavis: ‘I found in the first hour that he had nothing to teach me.’ ... Leavis was also told by Johnson: ‘At our first meeting he was teaching me.’ ... The difference is that Johnson’s remark was sardonic, Wittgenstein’s completely in earnest. It was actually Johnson who put an end to the arrangement...}}</ref> They had strong disagreements on logic and philosophy, but got on well when they did not speak about these things.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Britton |first=Karl |author-link=Karl Britton |url=http://archive.org/details/ludwigwittgenste0000fann |title=Ludwig Wittgenstein: the man and his philosophy |date=1967 |publisher=[New York] [Dell Pub. Co.] |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-391-00897-7 |editor-last=Fann |editor-first=K. T. |pages=61 |chapter=Portrait of a Philosopher |quote=He said how much he liked and admired Johnson and how well they got on as soon as they had decided to give up the philosophical questions. |url-access=registration}}</ref> Wittgenstein anonymously committed 200 pounds a year to a research fund for Johnson.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wittgenstein |first1=Ludwig |url=https://archive.org/details/letterstorussell00witt_0 |title=Letters to Russell, Keynes, and Moore |date=1974 |publisher=Cornell University Press |editor-last=von Wright |editor-first=G. H. |editor-link=G. H. von Wright |page= |pages=108, 121 |url-access=registration}}</ref> He was also kind to Johnson during his ill-health.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Malcolm |first=Norman |author-link=Norman Malcolm |date=1981-11-19 |title=Wittgenstein’s Confessions |url=https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v03/n21/norman-malcolm/wittgenstein-s-confessions |access-date=2026-04-02 |work=[[London Review of Books]] |language=en |volume=03 |issue=21 |issn=0260-9592 |quote=Although Wittgenstein had a poor opinion of W.E. Johnson’s three-volume work on logic, and Johnson in turn thought that Wittgenstein was arrogant and a disastrous influence in Cambridge, yet when Johnson’s health began to deteriorate ‘no one,’ says [[Maurice O'Connor Drury|Drury]], ‘could have shown more sympathetic solicitude than Wittgenstein did.’ He went frequently to Johnson’s home to play chess with him, and often was the audience while Johnson played Bach on the piano, since Wittgenstein knew that Johnson would not play unless he had a listener.}}</ref>

He died in [[St Andrew's Hospital]], Northampton, on 14 January 1931 and is buried at Grantchester, Cambridgeshire.<ref name=":0" />

==Work==
[[File:14. Members of the Moral Science Club, Cambridge, c. 1913.jpg|thumb|335x335px|Members of the [[Cambridge University Moral Sciences Club|Moral Science Club]] ''circa'' 1913, with W. E. Johnson sat in the middle of the front row (to the right of Bertrand Russell)]]
Johnson, who suffered poor health, published little. That, though "very able", he was "lacking in vigour" and had "published almost nothing" is a matter Bertrand Russell commented upon unsympathetically in a letter to [[Lady Ottoline Morrell|Ottoline Morrell]] of 23 February 1913.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Russell |first=Bertrand |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LU6heg3jfHcC&q=very+able%2C+but+lacking+in+vigour%2C+and+has+published+almost+nothing&pg=PA433 |title=The Selected Letters of Bertrand Russell. The Private Years, 1884-1914 |date=2002 |publisher=Routledge |others=Griffin, Nicholas. |isbn=0415260140 |location=London |pages=433–434 |oclc=49594254 |quote=W. E. Johnson ... is very able, but lacking in vigour, and has published almost nothing. His family make a cult of him, and talk as if having the ideas were everything, and writing them out a mere vulgar mechanical labour. It vexes me, because anybody who has ever written knows the intolerable labour of getting one's ideas into proper shape, long after they have seemed all right as mere thoughts. Universities are full of people who ought to write and don't — I always feel annoyed with them, and with people who minimize the labour of actually producing something.}}</ref> Johnson's obituary in ''[[The Times]],'' penned by [[J. M. Keynes]], more kindly reports that "his critical intellect did not readily lend itself to authorship."<ref name=":11">"W. E. JOHNSON," ''The Times'', 15 January 1931. Reprinted in {{Cite book |last=Keynes |first=John Maynard |url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Delphi_Collected_Works_of_John_Maynard_K/CQ3HEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=If+his+influence+on+Cambridge+thought+is+to+be+summed+up+briefly,+it+may+be+said+that+he+was+the+first+to+exercise+the+epistemic+side+of+logic,+the+links+between+logic+and+the+psychology+of+thought&pg=RA1-PT1869&printsec=frontcover |title=Delphi Collected Works of John Maynard Keynes (Illustrated) |date=2026 |publisher=Delphi Classics |isbn=978-1-80170-307-9 |language=en |author-mask=0}} and [https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/the-collected-writings-of-john-maynard-keynes/w-e-johnson/FD59AC065813A730BA015FFE3A31AC2F ''The Collected Writings of John Maynard Keynes'' (1978) pp''.'' 349–350] {{Doi|10.1017/upo9781139524230.037}} </ref> A memorial in ''[[Mind (journal)|Mind]]'' also proffered a charitable partial explanation of his reluctance to publish.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=D. |first=A. |date=1932 |title=W. E. Johnson (1858–1931): An Impression |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2250151 |journal=Mind |volume=41 |issue=161 |pages=136–137 |issn=0026-4423 |jstor=2250151 |quote=he gave above all the impression of one steadily pursuing his own way, and of not caring very much whether his views became known or not, or whether anyone agreed with him. It was the pure intellectual desire to reach truth, rather than the desire to-spread it or the hope of acquiring reputation, which seemed to drive him on. And this perhaps partly explains that reluctance to publish, which was in the end so fortunately overcome.}}</ref> In plainer terms, C. D. Broad wrote that Johnson "wrote much, but owing to ill-health and excessive diffidence and self-criticism he published very little."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Broad |first=C. D. |url=https://archive.org/details/britishphilosoph0000cama |title=British Philosophy in the Mid-Century: A Cambridge Symposium |date=1957 |others= |editor-last=Mace |editor-first=C. A. |editor-link=Cecil Alec Mace |page=23 |chapter=The Local Historical Background of Contemporary Cambridge |quote=Johnson was a most acute thinker and a very hard and conscientious worker. He wrote much, but owing to ill-health and excessive diffidence and self-criticism he published very little. After contributing a series of three important articles, entitled “The Logical Calculus,’ to the first three volumes of ''Mind'' in 1892 to 1894, he published nothing in philosophy until 1918, when he broke his long silence with two articles in ''Mind'' entitled “The Analysis of Thinking’. |url-access=registration |via=Internet Archive}}</ref>

Johnson's major publication was a three volume work ''Logic'' which was based on his lectures, Its volumes appeared, along with favourable reviews in the journal ''[[Mind (journal)|Mind]],'' in 1921,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gibson |first=James |date=1921 |title=Review of Logic: Part I. |url=https://archive.org/details/mindreview30edinuoft/page/448/mode/1up |journal=Mind |volume=30 |issue=120 |pages=448–455 |issn=0026-4423 |jstor=2249513 |via=Internet Archive}}</ref> 1922,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Broad |first=C. D. |date=1922 |title=Review of Logic, Part II. |url=https://www.stafforini.com/broad/Broad%20-%20Critical%20notice%20of%20Johnson's%20Logic.pdf |journal=Mind |volume=31 |issue=124 |pages=496–510 |issn=0026-4423 |jstor=2249771}}</ref> and 1924.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Broad |first=C. D. |date=1924 |title=Mr. Johnson on the Logical Foundations of Science |url=https://www.stafforini.com/broad/Broad%20-%20Mr.%20Johnson%20on%20the%20logical%20foundations%20of%20science%201.pdf |journal=Mind |volume=33 |issue=131 |pages=242–261 |issn=0026-4423 |jstor=2249779}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Broad |first=C. D. |date=1924 |title=Mr. Johnson on the Logical Foundations of Science (II.) |url=https://www.stafforini.com/broad/Broad%20-%20Mr.%20Johnson%20on%20the%20logical%20foundations%20of%20science%202.pdf |journal=Mind |volume=33 |issue=132 |pages=369–384 |issn=0026-4423 |jstor=2249554}}</ref>

This work may never have been published if it had not been for the efforts of [[Newnham College, Cambridge|Newnham]] student Naomi Bentwich (1891–1988).<ref name=":1" /> Bentwich persuaded him to publish, typed and co-edited the manuscript and encouraged him to finish the project. The preface to the first volume carries the acknowledgement: "I have to express my great obligations to my former pupil, Miss Naomi Bentwich, without whose encouragement and valuable assistance in the composition and arrangement of the work, it would not have been produced in its present form."<ref>{{cite book|last1=Johnson|first1=W. E.|title=Logic|url=https://archive.org/details/logic02john|date=1921|publisher=Cambridge University Press}}</ref> A fourth volume on probability was never finished, but parts of it would be published posthumously as articles in ''Mind''.<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":1" />

''Logic'' ensured his election to the British Academy and won him honorary degrees from the universities of Manchester and Aberdeen.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=William Johnson (1858-1931) |url=https://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Johnson.html |access-date=2019-06-21 |website=www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk}}</ref> Though conceding that ''Logic'' was "dated", even at publication, Sébastien Gandon argues that it would be unfair, given "the richness of his thought", to see Johnson "only as a member of the British logic 'old guard' pushed aside by the ''[[Principia Mathematica]]''" of [[Alfred North Whitehead]] and Bertrand Russell.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last=Gandon |first=Sébastien |url= |title=Early Analytic Philosophy – New Perspectives on the Tradition |work= |publisher=Springer International Publishing |year=2016 |isbn=9783319242149 |editor-last=Costreie |editor-first=Sorin |pages=269 |chapter=Wittgenstein’s Color Exclusion and Johnson’s Determinable |oclc=936040958 |quote=The book was already dated at the time of its publication. But seeing Johnson only as a member of the British logic 'old guard', pushed aside by the ''Principia Mathematica'', would be unfair and would not give credit to the richness of his thought. Indeed, many of Johnson's insights are today an integral part of philosophy. ... This is especially the case with Johnson's doctrine of determinable and determinate... |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gMdyCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA258}}</ref> Gandon contends that "many of Johnson's insights are today an integral part of philosophy" and that this is so especially of Johnson's doctrine of determinable and determinate.<ref name=":8" /> Johnson's work and influence in this latter regard is discussed in the ''[[Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]'' entry ''on Determinables and Determinates'' by [[Jessica Wilson]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Wilson |first=Jessica |title=Determinables and Determinates |date=2017 |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2017/entries/determinate-determinables/ |access-date=30 October 2025 |edition=Spring 2017 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}}.</ref><ref>Having also been discussed in that article's precursor ''[https://stanford.library.sydney.edu.au/archives/sum2010/entries/determinate-determinables/ Determinates vs. Determinables]'' by [[David H. Sanford]].</ref>

In his early work "The Logical Calculus" (1892), as [[Baruch Brody]] notes, he "developed an elegant version of [[Boolean algebra|Boolean]] propositional and functional logic, using conjunction and negation as his primitive symbols."<ref name=":10" /> It reveals the technical capabilities of Johnson's youth.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Passmore |first=John |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.135724 |title=A Hundred Years of Philosophy |date=1957 |publisher=Harmondsworth, Middlesex, England: Gerald Duckworth & Co. Ltd. |chapter=New Developments in Logic |chapter-url=https://archive.org/stream/in.ernet.dli.2015.135724/2015.135724.A-Hundred-Years-Of-Philosophy#page/n137/mode/2up/search/johnson}}</ref> The article begins as follows:

<blockquote>
"As a material machine economises the exertion of force, so a symbolic calculus economises the exertion of intelligence ... the more perfect the calculus, the smaller the intelligence compared to the results." 
</blockquote>

[[Arthur Prior|A. N. Prior]]'s ''Formal Logic'' cites this article several times.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Prior|first1=A. N.|title=Determinables, Determinates and Determinants|journal=Mind|year=1949|volume=58|issue=229|pages=1–20|jstor=2254522|doi=10.1093/mind/lviii.229.1|pmid=18113196}}</ref>

[[John Passmore]] tells us:
<blockquote>
"His neologisms, as rarely happens, have won wide acceptance: such phrases as "ostensive definition", such contrasts as those between ... "determinates" and "determinables", "continuants" and "occurrents", are now familiar in philosophical literature." (Passmore, 1957, p. 346)<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/stream/in.ernet.dli.2015.135724/2015.135724.A-Hundred-Years-Of-Philosophy#page/n5/mode/2up|title=A Hundred Years of Philosophy|last=Passmore, John|publisher=Gerald Duckworth & Co. Ltd.|year=1957|location=Harmondsworth, Middlesex, England|chapter=Some Cambridge Philosophers; and Wittgenstein's ''Tractatus''|author-link=John Passmore|chapter-url=https://archive.org/stream/in.ernet.dli.2015.135724/2015.135724.A-Hundred-Years-Of-Philosophy#page/n346/mode/1up}}</ref>

</blockquote>He is also credited with coining the term '[[Redundancy theory of truth|redundancy theory of truth']].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kunne |url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Conceptions_of_Truth/5KMUDAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PA36 |title=Conceptions of Truth |date=2003-06-05 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-924131-6 |language=en|first=Wolfgang|page=[https://archive.org/details/conceptionsoftru0000kunn/page/36/mode/1up 36]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Baldwin |first=Thomas |author-link=Thomas Baldwin (philosopher) |url=https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Moore_Arg_Philosophers/yhjGBQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PT327 |title=Moore |date= |publisher=Routledge |year=2010 |isbn=978-1-136-95777-2 |series=Arguments of the Philosophers |pages=327 |language=en}}</ref> Of his discussion of it, as Sahlin writes:<blockquote>W. E. Johnson in his ''Logic'' of 1921 discusses the eliminability of the predicate 'true'. According to Johnson, this predicate and its semantic import is best understood if it is compared with the functioning of the number '1' within arithmetic. Multiplying a number by 1 does not change anything, nor does adding 'it is true' to a sentence.<ref name=":9" /></blockquote>Ramsey, as Sahlin notes, likely wrote his more substantial remarks on the topic thinking a reference to Johnson superfluous.<ref name=":9" />

Of Johnson, Keynes writes:<blockquote>If his influence on Cambridge thought is to be summed up briefly, it may be said that he was the first to exercise the epistemic side of logic, the links between logic and the psychology of thought. In a school of thought whose natural leanings were towards formal logic, he was exceptionally well equipped to write formal logic himself and to criticise everything which was being contributed to the subject along formal lines.<ref name=":11" /></blockquote>

=== Economics ===
Johnson wrote three papers on economics. The first two, both published in the ''Cambridge Economic Club'', being 1891's "Exchange and Distribution"<ref>{{Cite book |last=Johnson |first=William Ernest |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/010613746 |title=Exchange and distribution. |date=1891 |location=Cambridge, Eng. |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref> and 1894's "On Certain Questions Connected with Demand"<ref>{{Cite book |last=Johnson |first=William Ernest |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/010613747 |title=On certain questions connected with demand |last2=Sanger |first2=Charles Percy |date=1891 |location=Cambridge, Eng. |via=HathiTrust}}</ref> (the latter being co-written with C. P. Langer).<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last=Moscati|first=Ivan|date=2005|title=W. E. Johnson's 1913 Paper and the Question of his Knowledge of Pareto|url=https://econwpa.ub.uni-muenchen.de/econ-wp/mhet/papers/0506/0506004.pdf|journal=Journal of the History of Economic Thought|language=en|volume=27|issue=3|pages=283–304|doi=10.1080/09557570500183553|s2cid=142585583|issn=1469-9656}}</ref> Of ‘The Pure Theory of Utility Curves’ (1913)<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=W. E. |year=1913 |title=The Pure Theory of Utility Curves |url=https://archive.org/details/WEJohnsonThePureTheoryOfUtilityCurves1913 |journal=The Economic Journal |volume=23 |issue=92 |pages=483–513 |doi=10.2307/2221661 |jstor=2221661}}</ref> [[William Baumol|Baumol]] & [[Stephen Goldfeld|Goldfeld]] (who reprinted all three papers with brief commentary) said it was "a considerable advance in the development of utility theory".<ref>{{cite book |title=Precursors in Mathematical Economics: An Anthology |date=1968 |publisher=London School of Economics and Political Science. |editor1-last=Baumol |editor1-first=W. J. |page=96 |editor2-last=Goldfeld |editor2-first=S. M.}}</ref> [[Joseph Schumpeter]] described it as an "important paper [that] contains several results that should secure for its author a place in any history of our science”.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Schumpeter |first=Joseph A. |author-link=Joseph Schumpeter |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/History_of_Economic_Analysis/HZ1WpT5cbgcC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=HISTORY+OF+ECONOMIC+ANALYSIS+JOSEPH+ALOIS+SCHUMPETER&printsec=frontcover |title=History of Economic Analysis |date= |publisher=Psychology Press |year=1954 |isbn=978-0-415-10892-8 |pages=1063 |language=en |quote=W. E. Johnson, "The Pure Theory of Utility Curves, Economic Journal, December 1913. This important paper contains several results that should secure for its author a place in any history of our science. But, having apparently been written in ignorance of Pareto's work, it aroused not unnatural resentment on the part of Italian economists because of its failure to acknowledge Pareto's priority in most essentials.}}</ref>

He wrote fourteen entries for the first edition of [[Inglis Palgrave|R. H. Inglis Palgrave's]] ''Dictionary of Political Economy'' (1894–1899)'','' mostly on economic method. He also lectured on mathematical economics from 1905–1922.<ref name=":7" /> He was of particular influence on [[John Maynard Keynes]]<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |title=Johnson, William Ernest {{!}} Encyclopedia.com |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/johnson-william-ernest |access-date=30 October 2025 |website=www.encyclopedia.com|last=Brody|first=Baruch|author-link=Baruch Brody}}</ref> and had been a colleague of his father [[John Neville Keynes]].<ref name=":1" />
